reasons: Only two of fifteen sections were reviewed here.

terms.meaning: tested across the whole path from input to final output, not one stage at a time
a fixed reference set of processes used to check the engine gives expected results
a built-in check that the engine's numbers are internally consistent and sensible
how much the final result moves when one input changes

used_by: Not visible in the files shown.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports the engine pieces under test
sections.what: Imports the engine's compute function, the engine input type, the prerequisite finder, the headline renderer and the sensitivity drivers, along with the test tools.
sections.why: Likely reason: each import is one piece of the engine these tests exercise.
sections.watch_out: Some imports were not seen in use within the supplied sections, so they may serve checks that were not reviewed.

sections.name: portfolio
sections.title: Builds the full value result once per session
sections.what: Builds the complete value result for the golden portfolio once, from the shared engine inputs, so every check that reads it sees the same result.
sections.why: Likely reason: the full computation is costly, and one shared result keeps the checks consistent with each other.
sections.watch_out: Every check reads the same object, so a check that alters it affects the rest.

sections.name: TestIdenticalInputsProduceIdenticalOutput
sections.title: Checks repeated runs give identical output
sections.what: Runs the same analysis twice and checks that the JSON text is exactly the same. It also checks that key totals are rounded to six decimal places before output.
sections.why: The class notes cite the project specification: two runs that disagree damage client trust faster than one wrong number.
sections.watch_out: Anything unordered, random, or a change in the order of adding numbers can break identical output.

sections.name: TestTheDiagnosticIsReal
sections.title: Checks the duplication figure is real
sections.what: Checks that the duplication ratio equals gross effort divided by deduplicated effort. Checks that the golden portfolio shows duplication above one, that deduplication removes effort, and that each shared capability has a pool equal to its largest claim with weights summing to one.
sections.why: The class notes say a ratio stuck at exactly one would make every deduplication test meaningless on real data.
sections.watch_out: The golden data must keep at least two processes sharing a capability, or these checks become empty.

sections.name: TestEveryFigureCarriesItsAssumptions
sections.title: Checks every figure states its assumptions
sections.what: Checks that the headline text names the duplication ratio, the depth tier and the evidenced share. Checks that every bridge currency appears in the headline. Checks that the assumptions list covers cost per FTE, horizon, wave length, prerequisite build effort and the function attribution gap.
sections.why: The class notes say the rule that every figure carries its assumptions is only enforced when a test checks the rendered text.
sections.watch_out: Renaming an assumption label will fail these tests even when the number is right.

sections.name: TestD12PrerequisitesAreNowPriced
sections.title: Checks prerequisite costs are priced and placed
sections.what: Checks that prerequisites are declared, that they appear on the bridge with a positive cost, and that each prerequisite is delivered in an earlier wave than the process that needs it, or in wave one. Also checks that each prerequisite is priced only once.
sections.why: The class notes say an earlier rule let a prerequisite land in the same wave as the process that needed it, which is only a name and not a real prerequisite.
sections.watch_out: Prerequisite declarations and the wave plan come from different sources, so they can disagree. This test is where that shows up.

sections.name: TestPhasingIsLiveOnRealData
sections.title: Checks phasing works on real data
sections.what: Checks that the golden portfolio spans more than one wave, that later waves start later, and that a process in a later wave realises less of its claim than it would in wave one, using the ramp function directly.
sections.why: The class notes say that before prerequisites pushed processes into later waves, everything sat in wave one, so phasing was never really tested.
sections.watch_out: The later-wave check recalculates expected values from the ramp function, so changing the ramp shifts the expected numbers too.

sections.name: TestSensitivityRanksSomethingReal
sections.title: Checks the sensitivity table is connected
sections.what: Checks that every driver appears in the sensitivity table, that at least one driver changes the answer, and that rows are sorted from largest swing to smallest within each currency.
sections.why: The class notes say that if every swing were zero, the drivers would not be connected to the result at all.
sections.watch_out: A sorted table can still contain wrong swing values. These tests only check connection and order.

sections.name: TestTheEvidencedShareIsWeightedByValue
sections.title: Checks the evidenced share is weighted correctly
sections.what: Checks that the evidenced share sits between zero and one, is below one on the golden data, that each wave reports its own share, and that at least one process is marked as unevidenced.
sections.why: The class notes say an evidenced share of exactly one would mean the calculation is not reading the records it claims to read.
sections.watch_out: These checks depend on the golden records keeping some unevidenced cases.

sections.name: TestConfidenceWideningReachesTheOutput
sections.title: Checks confidence widening reaches the output
sections.what: Checks that processes with zero confidence get a widening factor of four, and that no widening factor is below one, so widening never narrows a band.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the test itself. Likely reason: low-confidence estimates should be shown with wider ranges.
sections.watch_out: A factor below one would silently narrow ranges, which these checks are meant to catch.

sections.name: TestNoFieldNameClaimsMoreThanItComputes
sections.title: Checks field names match what is calculated
sections.what: Checks that realised effort equals credited effort times the realised fraction, and that the horizon factor is not multiplied in a second time. Also checks that the horizon factor's field description says it is a diagnostic and not a multiplier.
sections.why: The class notes say a field called adoption factor sat beside the horizon factor, suggesting a second multiplier that did not exist.
sections.watch_out: The field description text is checked directly, so rewording it can fail the test.

sections.name: TestAddingAProcessCannotDistortThePortfolio (part 1)
sections.title: Checks an added process cannot overclaim
sections.what: Builds a copy of a real process with a tiny claim, a huge baseline and a slow ramp, and checks that no process in the resulting portfolio is credited more than it claimed.
sections.why: The class notes describe the failure found in review: one small slow process cut the golden portfolio's gross benefit by 45 percent.
sections.watch_out: The helper that builds the extra process sets many fields by hand. Changing the data model may require changing it too.

sections.name: TestAddingAProcessCannotDistortThePortfolio: test_adding_a_process_moves_the_total_by_at_most_its_own_claim
sections.title: Checks adding a process moves the total only as much as its claim
sections.what: Adds the extra process and checks that the portfolio total moves by no more than that process's own claim. Also checks that the new process realises on its own ramp rather than on a shared schedule, and that the duplication ratio rises when a claimant is added.
sections.why: The class notes say that putting shared pools on one blended schedule would slow every other claimant of the same capability.
sections.watch_out: Credit can migrate between processes with different schedules and change the total. These checks catch that.

sections.name: TestAnUnpricedEstateSaysSo
sections.title: Checks missing prices are flagged
sections.what: Removes the inference prices from the cost basis and checks that the run cost breakdown is marked unpriced, that the bridge carries the same flag, and that the headline says UNPRICED and that the net benefit is an overstatement. Also checks that a priced basis shows no such warning, and that removing prices raises the net benefit.
sections.why: The class notes say an unpriced run shows a smaller cost and so looks like a cheaper system. This warning path had no test at all.
sections.watch_out: Unpriced results overstate the benefit. The headline text is what protects the reader.

sections.name: TestTheCostBandsReachRealOutput
sections.title: Checks cost ranges reach real output
sections.what: Checks that each bridge's net benefit range is wider than its gross benefit range, and that every nonzero cost line carries a range rather than a single point.
sections.why: The class notes say an earlier version gave every cost line as a single point, and a unit test passed only because it fed the helper inputs the pipeline never produced.
sections.watch_out: Tests on real output matter more than tests on helpers with invented inputs.

summary: Tests the whole value engine end to end on the golden portfolio, covering reproducibility, the diagnostic, prerequisite pricing, phasing, sensitivity, the evidenced share, confidence, field naming and cost bands.
purpose: Confirms that the complete engine, run on the golden portfolio, gives reproducible and honest results. The unit tests beside it check each stage alone and cannot show this.
why: The docstring says some properties only exist end to end, so they need a test that runs the whole chain.
how: Builds the value result for the golden portfolio once through a shared fixture, then runs checks that read that result. Only two of the fifteen sections were supplied, so the other checks are described only by their class names.
inputs: Engine inputs from the engine fixture in tests/value/conftest.py.
outputs: Pass or fail for each check.
risks: The file reads one shared result, so anything that changes it affects later checks. Most check bodies were not reviewed, so their meaning beyond their names is unverified.
debug: Start with the portfolio fixture and the compute function in packages/value/pipeline.py. Run a single test by itself to see whether a failure is caused by shared state.
